0.title: The Art and Science of Biblical Interpretation
0.essay:
Every time you open the Bible and ask, “What does this mean?”, you are interpreting. The question is not whether you will interpret Scripture, but whether you will do it carefully, consistently and faithfully. That is what hermeneutics — from the Greek word for “to interpret” — is about.

Why it matters

Most disputes in church history have been, underneath, disputes about interpretation. People usually agree on what the text says; they disagree about what it means and how it applies. How do the Old and New Testaments fit together? How should prophecy be read? What should Christians do with the laws of Moses? Learning to read well is not an academic hobby. The preacher or teacher who handles God’s word is handling a living sword, and a congregation that hears it rightly handled is being shaped by the only voice that can change a human heart.

The eight chapters

We begin with foundations: why interpretation is necessary and what guides it. Then the grammatical-historical method, the bedrock approach shared by evangelical readers of every tradition. Next, biblical theology: reading each passage within the whole story of the Bible. Then typology and prophecy: how the Old Testament anticipates and the New fulfils. After that, a respectful comparison of Reformed and Dispensational ways of reading. Then preaching and application: moving faithfully from the ancient text to people today. The last two chapters are practical tools: common exegetical fallacies to avoid, and the figures of speech and literary forms the Bible uses.

The aim is not cleverness but faithfulness — that God’s word would be heard as he spoke it, and obeyed.

1.title: Foundations: Why We Need Hermeneutics
1.essay:
“Just read it plainly,” some Christians say, as though the Bible interprets itself and the reader simply receives its obvious meaning. The instinct is reverent. But it misunderstands how language, history and our own minds work.

An ancient book

The Bible was written over some fifteen centuries, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, by about forty authors, in cultures very different from ours. It contains narrative, law, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, apocalyptic visions, letters and Gospels, and each kind of writing has its own conventions. A reader who ignores them will misread the text as surely as someone who reads a love poem as if it were a legal contract. Even Peter admitted that Paul’s letters contain “some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:16). Difficulty is not an embarrassment. It is an invitation to read more carefully.

Cutting it straight

Paul told Timothy, “Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). “Rightly handling” translates a word meaning to cut straight, like a craftsman cutting a true line or a builder cutting a straight road. Careless interpretation is not merely an intellectual failure; Paul calls it something to be ashamed of before God. And he calls the interpreter a “worker”: reading well is labour.

Scripture itself gives us an early picture of good interpretation. When Ezra read the law after the exile, the Levites “read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Read the text accurately, explain its meaning, help people understand — that is the task in three steps.

The Spirit and our minds

The Holy Spirit is the great interpreter of Scripture. Jesus promised, “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13). And without the Spirit, even brilliant readers miss the point: “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14). An unbelieving scholar can parse every Greek verb in John’s Gospel and still not receive it.

But the Spirit does not bypass our minds; he works through them. The Spirit who moved Paul to write a carefully argued letter to the Romans is not honoured by careless reading of it. Careful interpretation is not a lack of trust in the Spirit; it is the form that trust takes. So we pray before we read, and then we work.

Three guiding convictions

A text means what its author meant. Meaning is not whatever the reader makes of it. We seek what the human author, writing under God, intended to say.

God may mean more than the human author fully saw. Especially in prophecy, the divine Author can place in a text a depth of meaning that later Scripture brings out — never contradicting the original meaning, but filling it out.

Scripture interprets Scripture. The Reformers called this the analogy of faith. No passage stands alone; difficult texts are read in the light of clearer ones on the same subject. That keeps us from building a whole doctrine on one obscure verse.

Clear enough, and deep enough

The Westminster Confession speaks of the clarity of Scripture: the things necessary for salvation are so clearly set out that “not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them” (1.7). The Bible’s central message is plain enough for a child, and deep enough to reward a lifetime of study.

When Philip met the Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53, he asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” The honest answer was, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:30–31). The text was clear enough to raise the question, but he needed someone to show him how it fitted into the whole story — and Philip showed him Jesus. Every teacher of the Bible is called to be a Philip.

For reflection

Why is “just read it plainly” not quite enough? How do prayer and careful study work together in your own Bible reading? Can you think of a verse you once misunderstood because you read it out of context?

2.title: The Grammatical-Historical Method
2.essay:
The grammatical-historical method is the foundation of evangelical interpretation, shared by Reformed, Baptist, Lutheran, Anglican and Dispensational readers alike. It rests on two simple convictions: meaning is found in the words of the text, and those words were written in a real historical situation that shapes what they mean.

Grammar: attending to the words

God chose to speak in human languages, and the details matter: the meaning of a word, the tense of a verb, the force of a small connecting word, the shape of an argument. Every translation, however good, already involves interpretation, so careful readers make use of lexicons, grammars and good commentaries even if they do not read Hebrew and Greek themselves.

Small details can open up familiar verses. In Romans 3:23, “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God”, the verb “fall short” is present tense: we keep falling short. Sin is not only a past event in human history but our present condition — a continual failure to reflect the glory we were made to display.

Grammar also keeps us from claiming too much. In Ephesians 2:8, “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God”, the word “this” is neuter in Greek, while both “grace” and “faith” are feminine. So “this” refers to the whole package — salvation by grace through faith — rather than to faith alone. Other passages do teach that faith is God’s gift (Philippians 1:29), but this verse makes the broader point. Good interpretation lets grammar clarify, but does not build on grammar what it cannot bear.

History: hearing it as they heard it

Before we ask, “What does this mean for me?”, we must ask, “What did it mean for them?” Who wrote it, to whom, in what circumstances, and why? Paul’s letters were written to particular churches facing particular problems; Isaiah’s prophecies were addressed to particular kings in particular crises. When the Philippians heard Paul say “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20), they heard it as people proud of belonging to a Roman colony. Recovering that original hearing is the historical task, and our application grows out of it.

Isaiah 7:14 shows both sides at work. The prophecy of a sign — “the virgin shall conceive and bear a son” — was first given to King Ahaz during a war in 735 BC, and seems to have had some sign in his own day. Matthew applies it to the virgin birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:23). How the near sign and the final fulfilment relate is a question for the chapter on typology and prophecy. But we only see the question clearly by taking both grammar and history seriously.

Genre: knowing what kind of writing it is

Part of the historical task is recognising genre. Narrative works differently from a letter; poetry differently from law; apocalyptic visions differently from proverbs. Reading Revelation like a newspaper has produced endless date-setting and wild political speculation. Reading the Psalms as if they were doctrinal statements misses their character as inspired prayers. Even Genesis 1 raises genre questions that affect how we read the days of creation; the Creation and the Fall study sets out the views and argues for reading it as historical narrative of six ordinary days. Honest reading engages such questions rather than avoiding them.

One meaning, many applications

The grammatical-historical method holds that a text has one meaning — what its author intended — from which many applications flow. The literary scholar E. D. Hirsch put it well: meaning belongs to the author; significance belongs to the reader. This guards against two errors: allegory, which finds hidden spiritual meanings behind the plain sense, and reader-response approaches, which say a text means whatever it means to me.

Paul shows how a principle carries over. He quotes the law, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,” and asks, “Is it for oxen that God is concerned?” (1 Corinthians 9:9). He does not deny that God cares for oxen; he draws out the principle already in the law — workers deserve to share in the fruit of their labour — and applies it to gospel workers. That is controlled application, grown from the text’s own logic.

Careful reading settles many disputes before they start. At Pentecost, was the miracle in the speaking or in the hearing? Acts 2 says both: the disciples “began to speak in other tongues” (Acts 2:4), and the crowd heard them “each one… in his own language” (Acts 2:6). Close attention to the text comes before building a theology on it.

For reflection

Why must we ask what a text meant to its first readers before asking what it means for us? How does recognising genre change the way you read Revelation or the Psalms? What is the difference between meaning and application?

3.title: Biblical Theology: Reading the Whole Story
3.essay:
Systematic theology asks, “What does the whole Bible teach about this subject?” Biblical theology asks a different question: “How does the Bible’s teaching on this unfold, stage by stage, from Genesis to Revelation?” It reads Scripture as one story, told by one divine Author through many human authors, moving toward one climax: Jesus Christ.

One story with a shape

The Bible’s story has a clear shape: creation, fall, redemption, new creation. Every book and passage sits somewhere on that arc. So no text can be fully understood on its own. The sacrifices of Leviticus make full sense only when we see them pointing to Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice. David’s kingship makes full sense only as an anticipation of the eternal King. The exodus makes full sense only as the pattern for the greater exodus Jesus accomplished in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). A good reader always has peripheral vision: what came before this passage, and what comes after it?

Graeme Goldsworthy summed up the storyline as “God’s people in God’s place under God’s rule.” Eden had it. Israel had a partial version: God’s people, in the land, under his law. Christ fulfils it, and the new Jerusalem completes it. Almost any Old Testament passage can be placed on that line.

Jesus, the first biblical theologian

On the road to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Not just the obviously messianic passages — all the Scriptures. That is the charter for Christ-centred reading. Every part of the Old Testament says something about him, whether by promise, pattern, contrast or longing. Edmund Clowney traced the portrait as it grows: the offspring of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the blessing of Abraham (Genesis 12:1–3), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), the son of David (2 Samuel 7), the suffering servant (Isaiah 53), the Son of Man (Daniel 7). By the time we reach the Gospels, the New Testament is not a surprise; it is the answer to the question the whole Old Testament has been asking.

Built for Christ

Paul says “the law was our guardian until Christ came” (Galatians 3:24). The word describes a household slave who supervised a child until he came of age. The law was never meant to be the final form of God’s dealings with his people. It taught Israel the meaning of sacrifice and atonement, showed the shape of a holy life, and through Israel’s repeated failure prepared the way for the one who would perfectly obey and perfectly atone. The Old Testament is not merely earlier than Christ; it is structured for him.

Hebrews opens with the same conviction: God spoke “at many times and in many ways” through the prophets, “but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). The Son is not one more instalment; he is the destination.

Promise, pattern and covenant

The engine of biblical theology is promise and fulfilment. God makes promises — to Adam and Eve, to Abraham, to David — and the rest of Scripture traces them toward Christ. Alongside promises are patterns, or types: real people, events and institutions that God designed to foreshadow what was coming. Adam is “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14); the Passover lamb points to Christ (1 Corinthians 5:7); the tabernacle points to Christ’s body and the heavenly sanctuary (John 2:21; Hebrews 9:24). Typology is not allegory; it recognises patterns God himself wove into history, as the New Testament writers did.

Reformed biblical theology traces the story through the covenants: the covenant of works with Adam, and the one covenant of grace, administered through Noah, Abraham, Moses and David and fulfilled in the new covenant sealed with Christ’s blood. These covenants are not merely legal arrangements but the bonds by which God binds himself to his people.

Where the story is going

The end echoes the beginning: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3). Garden, tabernacle, temple, incarnation, the Spirit indwelling the church — all point to this final reality of God with his people, without veil or exile or sin. Read every passage in the light of where the story is heading, and familiar texts come alive.

For reflection

How would you summarise the Bible’s storyline in one sentence? Choose an Old Testament story you know well: where does it fit on the arc of creation, fall, redemption and new creation? How does it point forward to Christ?

4.title: Typology and Prophecy: Old Testament Anticipation
4.essay:
Matthew keeps saying that events in Jesus’ life happened “to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet”. Sometimes the connection puzzles modern readers. Was the prophet really predicting this? Understanding how the New Testament reads the Old requires two tools: typology, and a careful understanding of prophecy.

Fulfil, not abolish

Jesus said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). He did not cancel the Old Testament; he brought it to its intended completion. Its moral law still binds us; its ceremonies and its laws for the nation of Israel find their completion in Christ and his people. We neither throw the Old Testament away nor read it as though Christ had not come.

Patterns God placed in history

Paul explicitly reads the Old Testament typologically. After recounting Israel’s wilderness failures, he writes, “Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). The word translated “example” is typos, a pattern. God not only acted in history but ensured his acts were written down as patterns for later generations.

Hebrews says the earthly sanctuary was a copy of the true one: “Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself” (Hebrews 9:24). The builders of the tabernacle could not see all this; the Spirit reveals it later. Read Exodus and Leviticus with this in mind, and you find depths that repay a lifetime.

When a type is fulfilled, the fulfilment is always greater. The Passover lamb was real; the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world is far greater. Manna sustained life in the wilderness; the bread of life gives eternal life. The temple housed God’s presence behind a curtain; Christ is Immanuel, God with us, unveiled.

Prophecy with layers

Prophecy is direct prediction, and Old Testament prophecy often has layers: a near, partial fulfilment within Israel’s history and a final, full fulfilment in Christ. Theologians sometimes call this the “fuller sense”: God intends a depth of meaning beyond, but never against, what the human author fully grasped. Isaiah 7:14 is the classic case: Ahaz received a sign in his own day, but the true Immanuel, God really with us, came only at the incarnation.

Psalm 22 shows the same thing. David poured out real personal anguish: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The divine Author was also anticipating the cry of the Son of God from the cross. Both meanings are real; neither cancels the other. The fuller sense must agree with the plain sense, be drawn out by later Scripture, and follow the text’s own logic. It is not a licence for fanciful spiritualising.

Two test cases

“Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1) describes God calling Israel out of Egypt in the exodus. Matthew applies it to Jesus returning from Egypt as a child (Matthew 2:15). Hosea was not predicting Jesus’ childhood. Matthew is making a deeper point: Jesus is the true Israel, reliving Israel’s story and succeeding where Israel failed. That is typological fulfilment.

Isaiah 53 works differently. Centuries before the cross, it described a servant who “was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). In Isaiah 40–55 the servant is sometimes Israel, but here an individual suffers for the nation — innocent, bearing others’ sins, vindicated after death. The passage not only predicts the cross but interprets it in advance. When the Ethiopian asked whom the prophet meant, Philip answered: Jesus (Acts 8:32–35).

Reading out, not reading in

The New Testament writers were not reading the Old carelessly or creatively. They read it as Jesus taught them: as a book that at every level speaks of him. Christ-centred reading of the Old Testament is not reading foreign ideas into it, but the deepest kind of reading out — discovering what the divine Author placed there. Once we learn their patterns, they become our tools too.

For reflection

What is the difference between typology and allegory? How does Matthew’s use of Hosea 11:1 show Jesus as the true Israel? Why is the fulfilment of a type always greater than the type itself?

5.title: Reformed and Dispensational Hermeneutics: A Respectful Comparison
5.essay:
Two of the most influential evangelical ways of reading the Bible are the Reformed, or covenant, approach and the Dispensational approach. Both hold to the authority and inerrancy of Scripture, both use the grammatical-historical method, and both have produced faithful scholars and preachers. Their differences are real — but they are differences between people reading the same Bible seriously.

Three questions

The differences gather around three questions. How should the Old Testament promises to Israel be fulfilled? How consistently should a “literal” reading be applied, especially to prophecy? And what is the relationship between Israel and the church? These are not small questions; they shape how we read large parts of both Testaments. But the fact that godly, careful scholars have reached different answers should keep everyone humble.

The Reformed approach

Reformed interpreters read Scripture through the one covenant of grace, administered through the covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses and David and fulfilled in the new covenant. There is one people of God across the ages. The church, made up of Jews and Gentiles on equal terms, is the continuation and fulfilment of Old Testament Israel. Promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and his people: the land promised to Abraham widens into the inheritance of the whole renewed world (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:10, 16), and the throne of David is fulfilled in Christ’s present reign at the Father’s right hand. Paul’s words are central: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). Reformed Christians are usually amillennial or postmillennial.

The Dispensational approach

Dispensationalism was developed in the nineteenth century by J. N. Darby and spread through the Scofield Reference Bible and teachers such as Chafer, Ryrie and Walvoord. It insists that promises made to Israel must be fulfilled literally to ethnic, national Israel. Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with two programmes in God’s plan. The church was a “mystery” not revealed in the Old Testament (Ephesians 3:3–6), and will be removed at the rapture so that God can complete his purposes for Israel in the tribulation and a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, centred in Jerusalem. Progressive Dispensationalists (such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy) have softened the sharp distinction between Israel and the church while keeping a future for ethnic Israel and a literal millennium.

The texts in dispute

Both sides take Romans 11 seriously: “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). Both affirm God’s faithfulness to Israel. Dispensationalists see here a continuing national programme; Reformed interpreters see God preserving an elect remnant and, many believe, a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ within the one people of God. On “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26), some Reformed interpreters read “Israel” as all the elect, Jews and Gentiles; many others, including the Romans commentary in this app, read a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ.

In Ephesians 3:6 Paul says the mystery now revealed is “that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body”. Dispensationalists see the church as a new entity unforeseen in the Old Testament. Reformed readers note that Gentile blessing was always promised (Genesis 12:3); what was hidden was the manner — Gentiles included as full members of one body without first becoming Jews.

At Pentecost, Peter says David foresaw the resurrection of the Christ, who has now been exalted to God’s right hand (Acts 2:30–36). Reformed readers see the promise to David fulfilled in Christ’s present heavenly reign; Dispensationalists see a partial fulfilment, with an earthly throne in Jerusalem still to come. At the Jerusalem Council, James quotes Amos 9:11–12 about rebuilding “the tent of David” and applies it to the inclusion of the Gentiles (Acts 15:16–18). Reformed readers see fulfilment happening in the church; Dispensationalists see James finding a precedent in the passage rather than its primary fulfilment.

Weighing the evidence

Weighing the texts, the covenantal reading is the more faithful. The New Testament itself reads the promises to Abraham and David as fulfilled in Christ and in his one people of Jews and Gentiles (Galatians 3:29; Acts 2:30–36; Ephesians 2:11–22), while Romans 11 still holds out a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ.

Disagreeing as brothers and sisters

Where both views are present in a church, the wise course is to teach the texts honestly, set out the options fairly, say where you land and why, and keep the focus on the vast common ground: the authority of Scripture, the centrality of Christ, salvation by grace through faith, the certainty of the resurrection and the hope of Christ’s return. The differences are real. Our fellowship in the gospel is deeper still.

For reflection

What are the main differences between the Reformed and Dispensational approaches? How does Galatians 3:29 shape your understanding of who Abraham’s children are? How can Christians who differ on these questions honour one another?

6.title: Preaching and Application: From Text to Congregation
6.essay:
The purpose of interpretation is not academic but worshipful: that God’s people would hear God’s word and be changed by it. All the skills of careful reading serve one end — the living word reaching living people with clarity, power and love.

Crossing the bridge

Moving from the ancient text to people today is sometimes called crossing the bridge. There are two ditches. One is staying in the ancient world: a lecture on historical background that is interesting but never reaches the listener. The other is jumping straight to application without earning it from the text: relevant, perhaps, but not really biblical.

The bridge is theological. The same God who acted then acts now. The same word that addressed them addresses us. The same Spirit who inspired the text illumines us. The timeless truth of the passage, found by careful reading, carries us from then to now. Paul gives us permission and obligation at once: “whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4).

He also shows us how. Retelling Israel’s wilderness failures, he says, “Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did” (1 Corinthians 10:6). He does not say their situation is exactly ours; he identifies a pattern and shows how it speaks to us.

Three questions for every passage

Three questions keep application faithful. What does this passage reveal about God — his character, acts and purposes? What does it reveal about us — our sin, our need, our dignity? And where is the good news — how does this passage point to, or flow from, the gospel of Christ? A sermon or Bible study that answers all three, from the text, is a biblical one.

Haddon Robinson taught preachers to find the “big idea” of a passage — its one central claim — and let everything serve it. That is an interpretive discipline before it is a preaching technique: you cannot state the central idea until you have understood the text. Bryan Chapell, Edmund Clowney and others urged Christ-centred preaching: not forcing a gospel ending onto every sermon, but showing how each passage finds its fullest meaning in the story of redemption. Spurgeon is often quoted as saying that from any text he would make a beeline to the cross — not by skipping the text, but because every text belongs to the story of the cross.

Law and gospel

Every passage relates in some way to law (what God requires) and gospel (what God gives in Christ). It may convict, or comfort, or both in turn. The preacher who cannot tell which is which will produce either guilt without grace or grace without repentance. God’s people need both, rightly proportioned, from every text.

Reading the kind of language

Application depends on reading carefully. When Jesus says, “if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away” (Matthew 5:30), he uses deliberate overstatement, a common teaching device, to shock his hearers into attention. The point is not self-harm but radical seriousness about sin — dealing ruthlessly with whatever leads us into temptation. Recognising the kind of language Jesus uses is essential to obeying him rightly.

Doers, not only hearers

All interpretation serves obedience. “But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:22). Hearing without doing is self-deception: information without formation. The teacher’s work is not finished when the meaning is clear and the application stated. It is finished when the Spirit uses both to move hearers toward obedience — and that last step belongs to the Spirit.

That is also the great comfort. God says of his word, “it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose” (Isaiah 55:11). The sermon or study that is faithful to the text — however imperfectly delivered, however small the group — is a word sent by God. Our responsibility is faithfulness; the fruit is his. So, as Paul told Timothy, “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2), and trust the God who sent it.

For reflection

Which ditch are you more prone to: staying in the ancient world, or jumping to application too quickly? Take a passage you are reading this week and ask the three questions about God, us and the gospel. Where do you need to become a doer, not only a hearer?

7.title: Exegetical Fallacies: Mistakes to Avoid
7.essay:
Some of the most confident claims made from pulpits are simply mistaken. D. A. Carson’s Exegetical Fallacies catalogues errors that even well-trained readers make. Knowing them protects us from building sermons, and lives, on things the Bible never said.

The root fallacy

This is the assumption that a word’s true meaning lies in its origin. Preachers often say the Greek word for church, ekklēsia, means “the called-out ones,” because it comes from words meaning “out” and “call.” But in actual use it simply meant an assembly. Luke uses it of a riotous civic crowd in Ephesus: “the assembly was in confusion” (Acts 19:32). The church is indeed called out of the world, but that truth comes from other texts, not from this word’s pieces.

English shows the danger. “Nice” once meant foolish; “butterfly” has nothing to do with butter. Words mean what their users mean by them in context.

Semantic anachronism

This reads a later meaning back into an earlier word. Paul says the gospel is “the power of God for salvation” (Romans 1:16). The Greek word is dunamis, and some preachers say, “The gospel is God’s dynamite!” But dynamite was invented in the nineteenth century, and it destroys; Paul is speaking of God’s mighty power to save. Likewise, God loves “a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7); the Greek word is the root of “hilarious,” but Paul does not mean God wants us to laugh as we give.

The love fallacy

Perhaps the most common example is the claim that agapē always means a special, self-giving, divine love, while phileō means mere human affection. The words do overlap with that idea in many New Testament texts, but the distinction does not hold.

In the Greek Old Testament, the verb agapaō is used when “Amnon, David’s son, loved” his half-sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13:1), whom he then raped. Paul uses it of Demas, “in love with this present world” (2 Timothy 4:10), and Jesus of the Pharisees: “you love the best seat in the synagogues” (Luke 11:43). Meanwhile John uses both verbs for the same love: “The Father loves the Son” with agapaō (John 3:35), and “For the Father loves the Son” with phileō (John 5:20).

So what of John 21, where Jesus asks Peter, “Do you love me?” three times, twice with agapaō and once with phileō? Some still see a deliberate contrast. But John varies other words in the passage too (feed, tend; lambs, sheep), and his Gospel uses the two verbs interchangeably. The likeliest reading is that the point is not the vocabulary but the threefold question, which mirrors Peter’s threefold denial and restores him. What gives agapē its rich meaning is not the word, but what God did: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son” (1 John 4:10).

Illegitimate totality transfer

This loads every possible meaning of a word into each use. “Flesh” in Paul can mean the body, human nature, human weakness, or the sinful nature. To read all of these into every occurrence muddles the text. Each use must be read in its own context.

The word-concept fallacy

This assumes that if a word is absent, the idea is absent. The word “Trinity” never appears in Scripture, but the truth it names is everywhere. Conversely, a study of one word, such as “grace,” will not give the whole biblical teaching on grace, which appears in stories and pictures where the word is never used.

Grammatical fallacies

Some preachers claim that the Greek aorist tense always means a “once-for-all” action. It does not. The aorist simply presents an action as a whole, without describing how it unfolds. When Paul urges us “to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1), the aorist does not prove he means a single crisis moment rather than a lifelong offering. Grammar matters, but it must not be made to say more than it does.

Careless appeals to background

Historical background is a great help, but invented background is a great harm. It is often said that the “eye of a needle” in Jesus’ saying was a small gate in Jerusalem, which a camel could pass through on its knees. There is no evidence such a gate existed. And this reading destroys Jesus’ point. He meant something humanly impossible: “it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24). The disciples understood, which is why they asked who could be saved, and Jesus answered, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). The text does not mean salvation is difficult for the rich but achievable with effort. It means salvation is a miracle of God for anyone.

Logical fallacies

Readers often reason badly as well. A false either/or forces a choice the text does not require: is Jesus divine or human? He is both. Is salvation God’s work or our response? Scripture says both, in their proper order. Selective evidence, or proof-texting, builds a doctrine on the verses that support it while ignoring those that qualify it. And unwarranted links assume that the same word means the same thing everywhere, so that a meaning from one passage is imported into another.

Ignoring the context

The simplest fallacy may be the most common: lifting a verse out of its setting. “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13) is often claimed for sporting victories. But Paul has just said he has learned the secret of “facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need” (Philippians 4:12). He means Christ gives strength to be content in any circumstance. “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope” (Jeremiah 29:11) was spoken to exiles who would remain in Babylon for seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10). It is a promise of God’s faithful purpose for his people through long hardship, not a guarantee of personal success.

Why it matters

These mistakes are not harmless. A fallacy can make a sermon memorable while making it false, and it teaches people to trust clever tricks rather than the plain sense of God’s word. Good interpretation is humble. It lets God say what he said, which is always better than anything we could add.

For reflection

Have you heard or used any of these fallacies? Choose a favourite verse and read it in its full context. Does its meaning change?

8.title: Figures of Speech: How the Bible Uses Language
8.essay:
God spoke through human language, and human language is full of pictures, comparisons and turns of phrase. Recognising them is part of taking the Bible literally, because the literal meaning of a figure of speech is the meaning its author intended.

Figurative is not less true

When Jesus says, “I am the door” (John 10:9), no one thinks he is made of wood. Yet the statement is completely true. A figure of speech is not a way of saying something less real, but often a way of saying something more vividly. The question is never “literal or true?” but “what kind of language is this, and what does it mean?”

Simile and metaphor

A simile compares two things using “like” or “as.” The righteous man “is like a tree planted by streams of water” (Psalm 1:3). The Servant went “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7). A metaphor makes the comparison directly: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13); “The LORD is my shepherd” (Psalm 23:1). Ask what single point of likeness the author has in mind, rather than pressing every detail.

An extended metaphor develops one picture at length. Psalm 23 works out the shepherd image through a whole psalm. Ephesians 6 describes the believer’s armour piece by piece, and asks us to understand each piece: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God.

Metonymy and synecdoche

In metonymy, one thing stands for something closely associated with it. “They have Moses and the Prophets” (Luke 16:29) means the books they wrote. “The cup” at the Lord’s Supper means its contents. In synecdoche, a part stands for the whole. “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11) asks for every daily need, not only bread. “All flesh” often means all people.

Hyperbole

Hyperbole is deliberate overstatement to make a point unforgettable. “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother… he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). Jesus does not command hatred; Matthew records the meaning plainly: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Love for Christ must so outrank every other love that, by comparison, the others look like hatred. Recognising hyperbole keeps us both from dismissing such sayings and from misapplying them.

Personification and anthropomorphism

In personification, a thing is spoken of as a person. In Proverbs, wisdom “cries aloud in the street” (Proverbs 1:20). In anthropomorphism, God is described with human features: his arm, his eyes, his hand. God is spirit and has no body, but these pictures show his real power and attention. When Scripture says God “regretted” or “relented,” it uses human language to show that he truly responds to people, without implying that he learns, changes his mind about his purposes, or is surprised.

Irony and rhetorical questions

Paul rebukes the proud Corinthians with irony: “Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich!” (1 Corinthians 4:8). He means the opposite. A rhetorical question expects an obvious answer: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” (Romans 6:1). The answer follows: “By no means!”

Merism, idiom and euphemism

A merism names two extremes to mean everything between. “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) means the whole universe. “You know when I sit down and when I rise up” (Psalm 139:2) means all I do. An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words, like “lift up your head.” A euphemism softens something painful: believers who have died “are asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). That does not mean the dead are unconscious, as other texts make clear, but that death for the believer is temporary and will end in waking.

Hebrew poetry

Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas rather than sounds, in parallelism. Sometimes the second line restates the first: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1). Sometimes it contrasts: “A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother” (Proverbs 10:1). Sometimes it develops or completes the first. Seeing the parallel prevents us from building doctrines on what are two ways of saying one thing.

Other forms help too. A chiasm arranges ideas in a mirror pattern, A–B–B–A, often putting the main point at the centre: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). An inclusio brackets a passage with the same words, as Psalm 8 begins and ends, “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!” An acrostic begins each section with the next letter of the alphabet, as in Psalm 119 and Lamentations.

Parables

Parables usually make one main point, or a few, through a story from ordinary life. They are not allegories in which every detail stands for something. Augustine famously read the Good Samaritan so that the inn meant the church and the innkeeper the apostle Paul. That is not what Jesus meant. Jesus told the story to answer, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29), and ended, “You go, and do likewise” (Luke 10:37).

Apocalyptic symbols

Books such as Daniel and Revelation use symbols deliberately: beasts, horns, numbers and colours. They are meant to be decoded by the Bible’s own imagery, not by newspaper headlines. A lamb “standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6) is not a description of an animal, but a glorious picture of the crucified and risen Christ.

How to tell

Several questions help. Does the text signal a comparison with “like” or “as”? Would a literal reading be absurd, or contradict other Scripture? What kind of writing is this: narrative, poetry, parable, prophecy, apocalyptic? How do other biblical authors use the same image? And what did the original hearers most likely understand?

Above all, figures of speech are gifts. God did not give us a dry manual, but a book that speaks to imagination as well as mind, so that we might not only understand him but see his glory and love him.

For reflection

Which biblical picture of God — shepherd, rock, refuge, father, king — means most to you, and what single truth does it teach?
